paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar inputs requires both a score and a rule for deciding when that score warrants an alert. This paper studies the decision rule in the generalized BH algorithm, or g-BH. Its decisions use empirical p-values computed with a calibration set, making that reference data an important part of the detector.

The authors analyze how the calibration set affects detection performance. They show that the conditional expected true positive rate, given the calibration set, follows a beta distribution whose parameters depend on the prescribed level and calibration-set size. This connects variation in the reference data to variation in detection success and indicates that small calibration sets tend to hurt performance.

To address that problem, the paper introduces ensemble g-BH, which combines multiple empirical p-values when making decisions. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and show improvements over g-BH with small calibration sets. The contribution therefore concerns how available scores become decisions, with particular attention to situations where calibration data is scarce.
icml-2025-a-closer-look-at-generalized-b.tldr: Ensemble g-BH combines empirical p-values to improve out-of-distribution detection when calibration sets are small.

paragraphs: Fitting a flexible curve to noisy observations often requires choosing how much variation the curve should allow. The paper highlights that leading non-parametric regression methods need a tuning parameter matched to the unknown function’s smoothness to attain optimal rates. Knowing that smoothness effectively gives the method information about the process it is trying to estimate.

AKORN offers a parameter-free procedure for offline regression over functions with bounded TV1 variation. It feeds the available data through an optimal online denoising algorithm and uses detected change-points to choose spline knots. These knots mark where the fitted curve can change its behavior, allowing their placement to respond to the shape of the underlying signal.

The estimator combines passes through the data in both directions. Empirically, its performance is close to Trend Filtering even when that comparison method receives oracle knowledge of the true smoothness. The stated finding is a practical comparison: adaptive knot selection can approach that informed competitor without requiring the same smoothness-dependent tuning.
icml-2025-akorn-adaptive-knots-generated.tldr: AKORN uses online denoising to choose spline knots automatically, approaching oracle-tuned Trend Filtering in empirical performance.

paragraphs: An out-of-distribution score indicates how unusual an input looks, but a detector must still decide which inputs to flag. This paper focuses on that decision stage. It frames detection as online multiple hypothesis testing, where a sequence of incoming examples produces a sequence of statistical decisions.

The proposed generalized LOND algorithm, or g-LOND, controls the false discovery rate at a chosen level without requiring a particular dependence relationship between p-values. False discovery rate concerns the share of discoveries that are false, so this guarantee addresses the reliability of the collected alerts rather than only the quality of individual scores.

The authors also prove a separate result about false positive rate: under a generalized Gaussian-like distribution family, it converges to zero in probability. That distributional condition is part of the claim and should not be detached from it. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness for out-of-distribution detection. Together, the results make sequential decision-making a central design component alongside the score function.
icml-2025-an-online-statistical-framewor.tldr: g-LOND treats out-of-distribution detection as sequential testing with false discovery rate control and a conditional false positive convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning adapts an agent using a trajectory of interactions supplied as context, without updating its policy through gradients. This makes task inference crucial: the agent must work out what environment it faces from the available experience. Offline training makes this difficult because the training trajectories are fixed, while deployment contexts may follow different distributions.

The paper argues that many existing approaches learn approximate Bayesian inference tied to the training distribution. Their task estimates can consequently become sensitive to how the context was collected. Behavior-agnostic Task Inference, or BATI, instead uses a model-based maximum-likelihood approach that focuses on environment dynamics when inferring a task representation.

This focus is intended to separate information about the task from the behavior of the policy that generated the observations. In MuJoCo experiments, BATI interprets out-of-distribution contexts effectively and outperforms other methods even with substantial environmental noise. The results support dynamics-focused task inference as a way to improve robustness when deployment experience differs from the offline training data.
icml-2025-behavior-agnostic-task-inferen.tldr: BATI infers tasks from environment dynamics to make offline in-context reinforcement learning more robust to unfamiliar contexts and noise.

paragraphs: A model can answer a familiar symbolic problem correctly while depending heavily on the particular symbols it has seen before. This paper builds an evaluation framework that separates extracting an underlying pattern from applying rules to that pattern. Both abilities are needed for the paper’s definition of abstract reasoning.

The benchmark systematically changes the symbols used in rule-based tasks while preserving the structure being tested. It introduces two complementary measurements: Gamma tracks basic reasoning accuracy, and Delta measures dependence on particular symbols. Comparing performance under remapping gives the authors a way to assess whether success survives changes in surface representation.

Evaluations span commercial models, models with 7B–70B parameters, and multi-agent settings. They reveal weaknesses in non-decimal arithmetic and symbolic reasoning, with abstraction gaps persisting under chain-of-thought prompting. Delta also exposes performance degradation associated with operand-specific memorization. The findings suggest that strong results in familiar domains can coexist with fragile abstraction, and that testing invariance under symbol changes provides information beyond ordinary accuracy.
icml-2025-benchmarking-abstract-and-reas.tldr: A symbol-remapping benchmark separates reasoning accuracy from dependence on familiar symbols, revealing persistent abstraction gaps in evaluated language models.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because an agent receives little feedback about whether its actions are useful. Reward shaping adds feedback between those infrequent task rewards. The paper identifies a tension between rewarding novelty, which encourages exploration but can distract from the objective, and rewarding significant states, which supports stable convergence but can leave early exploration weak.

Dual Random Networks Distillation, or DuRND, combines these aims within one framework. Two lightweight random network modules produce complementary signals: a novelty reward for directed exploration and a contribution reward for progress toward completing the task. This gives the agent feedback about both encountering something new and moving toward its objective.

The authors report low computational overhead and strong performance in high-dimensional environments with sparse rewards, including Atari, VizDoom, and MiniWorld. DuRND outperforms several benchmarks in these evaluations. The findings support the value of coordinating exploration and task progress through a shared reward-shaping mechanism, rather than leaving either signal to carry the full learning problem.
icml-2025-catching-two-birds-with-one-st.tldr: DuRND uses two lightweight random networks to reward both novelty and task progress, improving learning in evaluated sparse-reward environments.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for combinatorial optimization face different obstacles as problems grow. Global prediction methods produce information about the whole solution, but overly smooth intermediate heatmaps can make long-range decisions difficult to decode. Local construction methods build solutions progressively, yet their autoregressive sequence of decisions becomes expensive on large instances.

COExpander implements Adaptive Expansion, a framework that combines global guidance with locally determined partial solutions. A global predictor learns under guidance from those partial solutions and produces informative heatmaps. These heatmaps then guide further expansion of the decided variables, with adaptive step sizes controlling how much the solution grows at each stage.

The paper also standardizes 29 benchmarks covering six optimization problems and instances ranging from 50 to 10,000 nodes. Experiments on this collection report state-of-the-art performance across the studied tasks. The contribution combines a solution-building strategy with a more consistent evaluation foundation: local decisions inform global predictions, and those predictions in turn help extend the partial solution at an adaptive pace.
icml-2025-coexpander-adaptive-solution-e.tldr: COExpander uses globally predicted heatmaps to expand partial solutions adaptively, reporting state-of-the-art results across standardized combinatorial optimization benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reasoning about causes can require combining several relationships rather than judging one relationship in isolation. This paper studies that combined ability as compositional causal reasoning: understanding how causal quantities compose as they propagate through a graph. Its goal is to make this capability systematically measurable in language models.

The evaluation framework covers two causal measures: average treatment effect and the probability of necessity and sufficiency. By examining how these quantities combine, it connects causal reasoning with the broader challenge of applying rules across multiple components. This provides a structured basis for analyzing errors, beyond recording whether a final answer is correct.

As a proof of concept, the authors evaluate models from the Llama, Phi, and GPT families on a math word problem. They identify several distinct categories of reasoning errors. Errors increase with causal-path complexity for every evaluated model except o1. That exception is part of the reported result; it does not establish that o1 is error-free. The study illustrates how an evaluation focused on causal composition can reveal differences in reasoning behavior.
icml-2025-compositional-causal-reasoning.tldr: A framework for evaluating causal composition finds distinct language-model error patterns and increasing errors with path complexity, except for o1.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter familiar attributes combined in ways that never appeared during training. The paper calls this compositional shift: some attribute combinations are entirely absent from the training distribution but present at test time. Handling this shift requires extending knowledge of the observed combinations to new ones.

The authors model the data using additive energy distributions, with each energy term representing an attribute. From this formulation they derive compositional risk minimization, or CRM. The procedure first trains an additive energy classifier to predict multiple attributes, then adjusts that classifier to address changes in which combinations occur.

The theoretical analysis establishes extrapolation to particular affine hulls of the observed attribute combinations, giving the result a specific geometric scope rather than a guarantee for every unseen combination. Benchmark experiments show improved robustness relative to methods developed for other subpopulation shifts. The work therefore links an explicit model of attribute composition to a training-and-adjustment procedure aimed at a demanding form of distribution shift.
icml-2025-compositional-risk-minimizatio.tldr: CRM uses additive attribute models and classifier adjustment to improve robustness to attribute combinations missing from training.

paragraphs: Choosing pretraining data by repeatedly training large language models is expensive. DataDecide studies whether smaller experiments can identify which datasets will produce stronger models at a larger scale. It releases models, data, and evaluations from controlled experiments across 25 corpora that differ in sources, filtering, and deduplication.

The experiments cover training data up to 100 billion tokens, models up to one billion parameters, and three random seeds. Ranking datasets using models at a single smaller size, such as 150 million parameters, predicts roughly 80% of pairwise comparisons correctly at the one-billion-parameter target. None of eight scaling-law baselines improves on the compute-versus-decision-quality frontier achieved by single-scale predictions.

The authors also find that continuous likelihood-based proxy metrics make several benchmarks more than 80% predictable at the target scale using just 0.01% of the compute. These findings support relatively simple small-scale comparisons within the studied setting. The released suite provides a shared basis for testing whether future prediction methods improve on that strong baseline.
icml-2025-datadecide-how-to-predict-best.tldr: DataDecide finds that small-model rankings strongly predict better pretraining datasets at its larger target scale, outperforming tested scaling-law methods on compute efficiency.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can adapt to a task by receiving demonstration examples in their input. This avoids fine-tuning, but adding many examples creates long inputs that demand substantial memory and computation. Efficient Multi-Modal Long Context Learning, or EMLoC, addresses that cost while retaining demonstrations as the basis for adaptation.

The method combines compression in chunks with adaptive token pruning at successive model layers. Compression produces compact memory representations tailored to the task. Pruning further reduces the tokens processed, under a Jensen-Shannon divergence constraint. Together, these operations reduce the amount of information the model must carry through its computation while seeking to preserve useful task evidence.

Across diverse vision-language benchmarks, EMLoC matches or exceeds the performance of naive long-context approaches while substantially reducing inference complexity. The reported results support combining compression and pruning for training-free adaptation, particularly when long demonstration contexts would otherwise be costly. The contribution centers on making example-based adaptation more computationally practical without requiring a separate round of model fine-tuning.
icml-2025-efficient-multi-modal-long-con.tldr: EMLoC compresses demonstrations and adaptively prunes tokens to make training-free multimodal adaptation more efficient while preserving benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Graph attention lets a model vary how strongly it uses information from different neighbors. This paper asks when that flexibility helps node classification. Its theoretical analysis uses contextual stochastic block models and distinguishes noise in the graph’s connections from noise in the features attached to its nodes.

Within this framework, attention can improve classification when structural noise exceeds feature noise. When feature noise dominates, simpler graph convolutions are more effective. The paper also studies over-smoothing, where repeated processing makes node representations insufficiently distinct. In a high signal-to-noise regime, the analysis shows that attention can resolve over-smoothing that affects graph convolutional networks.

These findings motivate a multi-layer graph attention architecture with a weaker signal-to-noise requirement for perfect classification in the studied graph model. The threshold changes from omega of the square root of log n to omega of that quantity divided by the cube root of n. Synthetic and real-world experiments corroborate the theoretical insights. The central implication is conditional: attention’s value depends on the graph’s noise structure and the operating regime.
icml-2025-graph-attention-is-not-always-.tldr: The analysis shows that graph attention’s benefits depend on structural versus feature noise and derives improved classification conditions for a multi-layer architecture.

paragraphs: Proteins can adopt multiple conformations, and their motion can matter for function. A single predicted structure does not capture that diversity. This paper develops a framework for generating ensembles of protein structures that agree with experimental measurements, bringing observed conformational variation into the prediction process.

The framework treats a structure predictor such as AlphaFold3 as a sequence-conditioned prior: a starting distribution over plausible structures for a given protein sequence. Experimental measurements then inform posterior inference over structures. This formulation makes ensemble construction an inverse problem, using measurements to infer the conformations that could explain them.

Real-data experiments demonstrate several uses. The method recovers previously unmodeled variation from crystallographic densities, produces high-accuracy NMR ensembles orders of magnitude faster than existing practice, and incorporates pairwise cross-link constraints. The authors report that their ensembles outperform AlphaFold3 and sometimes fit measurements better than deposited PDB structures. These results support combining structural prediction with experimental evidence to represent multiple conformations, with the better fit to deposited structures explicitly occurring only in some cases.
icml-2025-inverse-problems-with-experime.tldr: The framework combines protein structure predictors with experimental measurements to infer conformational ensembles that better capture observed structural diversity.

paragraphs: Mixed-precision quantization assigns different numerical bit widths to different network layers. Choosing that assignment can be expensive when the search uses a large dataset. This paper instead searches on a small dataset and transfers the resulting strategy to a larger one, requiring model weight adjustment without a large-scale quantization fine-tuning process.

Three optimization techniques support the transfer. Sharpness-aware minimization aims to improve generalization of the quantized model. Implicit alignment of gradient directions addresses conflicts between optimization objectives. An adaptive perturbation radius accelerates optimization. Together, these mechanisms target both the quality of the transferred strategy and the computational cost of finding it.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and experiments. Searching on CIFAR10, described as 0.5% of ImageNet’s training-data size, yields equivalent ImageNet accuracy at substantially lower computational cost. They report efficiency improvements of up to 150% over the baselines. The result suggests that a carefully designed small-dataset search can provide useful layerwise precision decisions for the larger evaluated task.
icml-2025-learning-from-loss-landscape-g.tldr: The method transfers mixed-precision strategies found on small datasets to larger tasks, preserving reported accuracy while reducing search cost.

paragraphs: Optimal stopping asks when an agent should stop rather than continue. This paper extends the problem to cooperating agents in a finite-space, discrete-time environment. Directly solving their joint stopping problem becomes computationally prohibitive when the population is very large, motivating a description based on the population’s limiting behavior.

The authors study mean-field optimal stopping, obtained as the number of agents tends to infinity. They establish that it approximates the multi-agent problem well and prove a dynamic programming principle using mean-field control theory. This gives a mathematical foundation for replacing a large collection of interacting stopping decisions with a more scalable formulation.

Two neural-network methods solve the resulting problem. One learns stopping decisions from simulated full trajectories. The other uses the dynamic programming principle to estimate values and learn stopping rules through backward induction. Numerical experiments on six problems, with spatial dimension up to 300, demonstrate effectiveness and scalability. The contribution combines an approximation result, a recursive solution principle, and practical learning methods within the stated discrete-time, finite-space setting.
icml-2025-learning-to-stop-deep-learning.tldr: A mean-field formulation and two deep learning methods make cooperative optimal stopping tractable for large agent populations in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Training and evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning requires difficult problems with useful solutions. Creating these at scale demands expert effort, while older evaluation problems may already appear in model training data. This paper addresses both issues using problems and community solutions from the Art of Problem Solving forum.

An automated pipeline uses open-source language models to extract question-answer pairs. The resulting AoPS-Instruct dataset contains more than 600,000 pairs, and fine-tuning on it improves reasoning performance across several benchmarks. A related pipeline builds LiveAoPSBench, an evolving evaluation set that uses timestamps and recent forum material to make contamination more difficult.

The authors observe a substantial decline in model performance over time across the evaluation material. They interpret this as suggesting that success on older examples may partly reflect pretraining exposure rather than reasoning alone. That interpretation remains a suggestion, not proof about any individual answer. The overall contribution couples a scalable source of training examples with a continually refreshed evaluation process for advanced mathematical reasoning.
icml-2025-leveraging-online-olympiad-lev.tldr: Automated AoPS extraction produces a large math-training dataset and an evolving benchmark that probes possible effects of prior training exposure.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, such as mappings associated with partial differential equation solutions. Their predictions can be useful for simulation, but consequential applications also need information about predictive error. LUNO adds approximate Bayesian uncertainty quantification to an already trained neural operator.

The method linearizes the model and propagates Gaussian uncertainty over its weights into uncertainty over predicted functions. The resulting belief is a function-valued Gaussian random process. This creates a theoretical bridge from existing Bayesian deep learning techniques, including the linearized Laplace approximation, to models whose outputs are functions rather than fixed collections of numbers.

LUNO preserves the underlying neural operator’s resolution-agnostic design, so its uncertainty framework is not tied to one output resolution. It can be applied after training without retraining the network, adds little prediction overhead, and scales to large models and datasets. A Fourier neural operator case study evaluates these properties. The contribution is a practical route to approximate uncertainty estimates, grounded in a probabilistic interpretation of the linearized operator.
icml-2025-linearization-turns-neural-ope.tldr: LUNO converts Gaussian weight uncertainty into function-valued predictive uncertainty for trained neural operators through linearization.

paragraphs: Increasing the size of a deep reinforcement learning network does not automatically make it easier to train or more effective. The paper connects this difficulty to training pathologies that have motivated interventions such as periodic resets and layer normalization. It investigates whether a simpler structural change can improve scaling.

The proposed change is static random sparsity. Before training begins, a predetermined fraction of weights is randomly removed in a single pruning step. The authors show that this alone can provide additional scaling potential beyond dense counterparts using state-of-the-art architectures. Their analysis finds greater parameter efficiency for expressivity and stronger resistance to optimization problems, including loss of plasticity and interference between gradients.

These findings connect network connectivity to both what a model can represent and how well it continues learning. Evaluations extend to visual and streaming reinforcement learning, where sparsity shows consistent benefits. The stated result supports one-time random pruning as a useful scaling intervention in the tested settings, without requiring an increasingly elaborate training modification.
icml-2025-network-sparsity-unlocks-the-s.tldr: Removing random weights once before training improves the scaling and optimization behavior of evaluated deep reinforcement learning networks.

paragraphs: Many-shot jailbreaking tests a vulnerability in models that accept long contexts: fabricated conversational history can make harmful compliance appear to be an established pattern. This paper studies how the content and selection of that history affect the success of such attacks against language-model safety alignment.

PANDAS combines three modifications named positive affirmations, negative demonstrations, and adaptive sampling. The sampling component is tailored to the target prompt’s topic, making the supplied examples more deliberately selected than a random collection. The paper also introduces ManyHarm, a dataset of harmful question-answer pairs used in studying this attack setting.

Extensive experiments show that PANDAS significantly outperforms baseline methods in long-context scenarios. The authors additionally analyze attention to investigate how the context vulnerability is used and how their modifications improve attack performance. The findings identify fabricated conversational context as an important object of safety evaluation: both the structure of the examples and their relationship to the target topic can affect the behavior of the tested models.
icml-2025-pandas-improving-many-shot-jai.tldr: PANDAS improves many-shot jailbreak performance through modified fabricated dialogues and topic-adaptive example selection in evaluated long-context scenarios.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using data encountered during inference. Some incoming samples help this process, while others undermine optimization. Existing approaches often filter out the latter, but doing so discards potentially useful information. PTTA studies whether those harmful-to-adaptation samples can instead be transformed into useful training material.

Its purification strategy uses a saliency indicator to characterize benign and malicious samples. It retrieves benign examples with opposite effects on the objective function and combines them with malicious examples through Mixup. The resulting purification loss can be added to existing adaptation algorithms, without requiring careful adjustment of the sample-selection threshold.

The authors report improved online test accuracy and effective use of information that would otherwise be discarded. Experiments cover four types of test-time adaptation tasks, as well as classification, segmentation, and adversarial defense. The contribution is a plug-in strategy for changing how adaptation handles problematic observations: it attempts to repair their optimization effect so that more of the available test data can contribute.
icml-2025-ptta-purifying-malicious-sampl.tldr: PTTA mixes problematic test samples with selected benign examples to improve their usefulness for test-time adaptation.

paragraphs: Spatiotemporal graph models predict patterns that vary across both connected locations and time. The paper identifies a weakness in conventional node-to-node messaging: predictions can become sensitive to shifts in those spatial and temporal patterns. STOP addresses this by changing how information moves through the model and how training environments are constructed.

Its centralized messaging mechanism uses Context-Aware Units to exchange coarse-grained spatiotemporal features with nodes, blocking conventional direct node-to-node messages. A second mechanism perturbs these messages to create variant environments. Training across those variations encourages the extraction of contextual features that generalize across changes.

The method also uses a spatiotemporal distributionally robust optimization approach to expose the model to challenging environments. Across six datasets and comparisons with 14 baselines, the authors report improvements of up to 17.01% in generalization performance and 18.44% in inductive learning performance. These are reported maxima, rather than uniform gains across all evaluations. The results support combining centralized interaction, message variation, and robust optimization to improve prediction under distribution shifts.
icml-2025-robust-spatio-temporal-central.tldr: STOP combines centralized messages, message perturbations, and robust optimization to improve spatiotemporal prediction under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes more demanding as tasks involve more agents and longer histories. A useful model must preserve decision quality while controlling the memory needed to process their observations. Sable addresses these requirements through a sequence-modeling approach designed for multi-agent observations and temporal reasoning.

The method adapts the retention mechanism from Retentive Networks. This provides computationally efficient processing together with long-context memory, allowing the model to use information across time. The architectural aim is to make access to that history compatible with larger agent populations, so that temporal reasoning does not prevent scaling.

Across six environments, Sable significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on 34 of 45 tested tasks. It also maintains performance in scaling experiments involving more than a thousand agents, with memory usage increasing linearly. Ablations investigate the sources of its gains and confirm its efficient memory use. The results support the combined performance and scalability claims within these evaluations, while the task count makes clear that the reported superiority is not universal.
icml-2025-sable-a-performant-efficient-a.tldr: Sable adapts retention-based sequence modeling for multi-agent learning, improving most tested tasks and scaling beyond a thousand agents with linear memory growth.

paragraphs: Density-based mode-seeking methods connect lower-density points toward higher-density neighbors, then identify peaks that can organize clusters. Deciding which connections to break often depends heavily on local characteristics. This can require thresholds chosen separately for each dataset or human intervention to obtain useful clusters.

TANGO introduces typicality, a measure of confidence that a point should count as a mode. It derives this measure by examining locally defined dependencies from a global perspective. An accompanying algorithm uses typicality to identify modes efficiently, bringing information from the broader dependency structure into what would otherwise be a locally driven decision.

The clustering procedure then uses graph-cut optimization with an improved path-based similarity to assemble the final groups. The paper includes theoretical analysis of its algorithm and evaluates TANGO on synthetic and extensive real-world datasets, reporting effectiveness and superiority in those experiments. Its contribution joins two stages: identifying representative density peaks through a global view and assigning data to final clusters through graph-based optimization.
icml-2025-tango-clustering-with-typicali.tldr: TANGO identifies density modes using globally informed typicality and forms clusters with path-based similarity and graph-cut optimization.

paragraphs: In multivariate forecasting, different variables may influence the target over different time intervals. The paper calls this the multi-delay issue. Processing every variable or time point uniformly can obscure those differences, weakening a model’s ability to represent both relationships between variables and the timing of their effects.

TimePro is a Mamba-based model that builds states sensitive to both variable identity and time. It preserves detailed temporal features within each variable token and adaptively selects relevant time points to modify the ordinary state. The resulting hyper-state combines information about variable relationships with information about salient moments.

This construction matters because useful forecasting evidence depends on both which variable carries a signal and when that signal occurs. Experiments across eight real-world long-term forecasting benchmarks show competitive performance with linear complexity. The stated finding supports the efficiency and usefulness of this joint representation in the evaluated tasks; it does not claim that TimePro wins on every benchmark. The model’s main contribution is selective temporal processing within a representation that also captures relationships across variables.
icml-2025-timepro-efficient-multivariate.tldr: TimePro builds variable- and time-aware states to address differing temporal influences, achieving competitive long-term forecasting with linear complexity.

paragraphs: A tumor segmentation shows where a model places a boundary, while a textual explanation describes why a finding may be meaningful. The paper aims to connect these outputs: models should justify detection or segmentation using clinical concepts and identify the corresponding visual evidence. This addresses the weak link between internal representations and clinically meaningful explanations.

The authors first build a dataset of 180,000 image-mask-rationale triples, with quality evaluated by expert radiologists. These paired examples connect images and spatial annotations with written reasoning. They then introduce rationale-informed optimization that separates fine-grained clinical concepts and localizes them through self-supervision, without requiring pixel-level annotations for each concept.

Experiments across medical benchmarks report superior segmentation, detection, and additional task performance. The methodological contribution is the combination of rationale data and training that grounds concepts spatially. It provides a way to make a model’s clinical language refer to visible evidence, while also improving the evaluated prediction tasks. The stated findings concern benchmark performance and grounded explanation, rather than establishing clinical trust as a measured outcome.
icml-2025-why-is-there-a-tumor-tell-me-t.tldr: The paper combines image-mask-rationale data with rationale-informed training to connect tumor predictions, clinical concepts, and localized visual evidence.
